About

I’m Obada Al-Taani, a design student at Jordan University of Science and Technology, in the Department of Design and Visual Communication. My work sits between UX/UI design and game design. I research the people I design for, plan the structure first, then build the look and the rules. This portfolio shows three projects: Navi, a guide app for university freshmen; Volt Escape, a first-person puzzle game about light; and Reno, a bilingual Arabic and Latin typeface built on one grid.

Let’s build something worth exploring.

Key decisions

Light as the core mechanic

TriedA standard “find the code, type it in” escape room

ChoseCodes that appear only under the flashlight, with a limited battery

WhyDarkness becomes part of the puzzle instead of just a mood.

No combat

TriedCombat and chasing enemies

ChoseEnvironmental hazards and a failing facility AI

WhyThe target audience prefers logic over action.

Three levels that build up

TriedOne big puzzle space

ChoseA teach, test, pressure order: simple codes, multi-room chains, then time pressure

WhyEach level adds exactly one new kind of pressure.

Read the full story
01

The idea

Volt Escape is a first-person escape-room puzzle game set in a decaying power plant. The player is a lone technician who wakes up lost and must find the code that opens each electronic door before the meltdown. There is no combat. The twist is that light is a tool: some codes only appear under the flashlight beam or from certain angles, and the battery is limited, so every second of light has a cost. The look is “industrial cyberpunk”, with rusted metal and concrete against neon glow.

02

My role

Lead game designer and concept developer, for DV362 Introduction to Computer Games. I defined the concept, premise and three-level structure, wrote the Game Design Document, built the pitch deck, and collected the visual references. The corridor and room photos are references that set the mood, not my own work.

03

The process

The project grew from one idea into a set of documents. I began with the core idea and premise, then defined the visual style and gathered references for each location. After that I designed the protagonist and his tools, the investigation mechanic, and a four-step gameplay loop: explore, obstacle, deduction, reward. Finally I planned three levels, each adding one new pressure: the Control Room teaches the flashlight and 3-digit codes, The Grid asks the player to link clues across rooms, and The Core adds time pressure.

05

The outcome

The result is a complete concept package: a 10-slide pitch deck and a Game Design Document for a game that can be understood from one image and one sentence, yet has enough depth for several levels. The game is not built yet. The next step is playtesting how easily players find hidden codes and how the battery feels.

Key decisions

Color and typography

TriedSeveral fonts and blues from the mood board (Onsor, Anmaat, Minimal Fonts, Inter)

ChoseModern shades of blue with Inter

WhyBlue builds trust, and Inter stays readable on every screen size.

App structure

TriedAll services together on one page

ChoseFive sections, a bottom navigation bar, and a study plan split by year and semester

WhyIt reduces clutter and keeps everything one tap away for a student who does not know the system yet.

The “Ask” feature

TriedReady-made FAQs only

ChoseDirect chat or call with experienced students, alongside FAQs and tips

WhyA new student trusts someone who went through the same stage.

Read the full story
01

The idea

Navi is a mobile app that simplifies university life for students in Jordan. It brings together university and major search, a study plan tracker from Year 1 to Year 6, interactive campus maps, and an “Ask” section where students chat or call experienced students. Research showed that most freshmen (“Sanafeer”) feel lost in their first semester, and existing apps offer fragmented services. Navi turns that confusion into a guided experience.

02

My role

UX/UI designer and researcher. I did the research, competitor analysis, personas, sitemap, wireframes, visual identity (logo, colors, typography), and the final screens and mockup.

03

The process

I started with name research, a competitor analysis and three personas: a high school graduate, a current student, and a student navigating a large campus. Then I built a mood board and analyzed each reference for color, font, layout and icons. Next came a sitemap with five sections, low-fidelity wireframes, Arabic right-to-left layouts, and finally the final screens and mockup.

05

The outcome

Navi is a complete, consistent design, from research to final screens and mockup. Its strength is one place for the study plan, campus map and peer support, built around the real needs of Jordanian students.

RenoAn Arabic and Latin typeface built from the grid of a solar cell

RoleTypeface designer, Arabic and LatinDeliverablesProcess book and final posterBuilding unit6 cm × 6 cm grid
The sourceSolar cell grids
The systemOne grid, two scripts
The setLetters grouped by shape
  1. Inspiration
  2. Grid
  3. Building units
  4. Letter families
  5. Poster
Read the full story
01

The inspiration

Reno takes its shapes from the geometry of high-efficiency solar cells. The fine lines of a cell’s metal contact grid collect and carry electrons, and their precision keeps the path short and the energy loss low. The diagonal patterns that bounce sunlight back into the cell gave the typeface its angles.

02

The building unit

A single geometric grid is the foundation for both the Arabic and the Latin letters. Each letter is drawn inside a fixed 6 cm by 6 cm square, so the grid decides the paths, angles and balance. The intersecting lines echo the conductive fingers of a photovoltaic panel.

03

The letter families

The Latin letters are sorted into three families: vertical, curved and sharp. The Arabic letters are sorted by shape too: vertical, curved, horizontal and descending. Guide lines for cap height, x-height and baseline keep both scripts aligned.

04

The outcome

The project ends in a 27-page process book that shows every letter on its grid, and a final set of three sheets, including a poster that sets one line in Latin and Arabic side by side.
